claims.text: A continuous-composition-gradient thin film can be synthesized for the HfNbTaTiZr alloy system.
Local changes in the percentage of an individual constituent, such as Hf, will correlate with systematic changes in hardness.
The deposited HfNbTaTiZr thin film has an initially uniform microstructure.
Combinatorial thin-film deposition can produce a library that systematically varies the percentages of HfNbTaTiZr constituents.
Localized nanoindentation can measure mechanical-property variations across the compositional-gradient library.
Elemental-concentration gradients across the film lead to local microstructural variations.
Changes in local HfNbTaTiZr composition can modify the local phase distribution.
Changes in local composition can modify grain size.
Changes in local composition can cause secondary phases to form.
Composition-induced changes in phase distribution and microstructure affect hardness.
Regions with a higher concentration of a selected element will have a statistically measurable hardness difference from regions with a lower concentration.
Regions near the nominal average HfNbTaTiZr composition provide a baseline comparable to conventionally synthesized HfNbTaTiZr.
Substrate effects or extreme film-thickness variations may alter the observed mechanical-property trends.
The quantitative relationship between individual elemental percentages and mechanical-property changes cannot be specified a priori because of interactions in the multicomponent alloy.
EDS or XRF can determine local elemental composition along the gradient.
SEM or TEM can characterize local microstructure along the gradient.
Failure to detect a consistent composition-hardness relationship at p < 0.05 is defined as falsifying the proposed significant influence of constituent percentages.
